test_title: RRB ALP CBT-II (Machinist) Official Paper (Held On: 06 May, 2025 Shift 1)
subject: general
question: Which of the following is a characteristic of a flat drill?

options.text: It is primarily used for deep-hole drilling with high efficiency.
It features parallel and taper shank designs for various applications.
For the smooth ejection of the chip, it features a helical groove running along its length.
Its production is inexpensive, but its chip removal capability is poor.

solution:
**Concept**

 
• A flat drill is one of the simplest types of drilling tools, typically forged from a single piece of tool steel or high-speed steel.
 
• Unlike twist drills, flat drills do not possess helical flutes (grooves) along their body.
 
• The primary design of a flat drill consists of a flat blade with two cutting edges.

**Key Characteristics**

 
• **Manufacturing:** They are very easy and inexpensive to produce compared to twist drills.
 
• **Chip Disposal:** Because they lack helical flutes, there is no natural path for chips to be lifted out of the hole. This leads to poor chip removal and frequent clogging.
 
• **Application:** They are generally used for drilling shallow holes in wood or soft metals, or for specialized sizes where a twist drill is unavailable.
 
• **Heat Dissipation:** Due to the lack of flutes and proper clearance, these drills tend to overheat quickly during operation.

**Explanation**

When analyzing the characteristics of a flat drill, we compare its design to the more common twist drill:

 
• Twist drills feature **helical grooves** (flutes) that act as a screw conveyor to automatically eject chips. Flat drills do not have this feature, meaning chips stay in the hole, leading to poor efficiency and potential damage if used for deep holes.
 
• Flat drills are essentially a flat piece of metal ground to a point. This simplicity makes them **inexpensive to manufacture**.
 
• Shank designs (parallel or taper) are common to almost all types of drills to allow them to fit into different chucks or spindles, but they are not the defining "characteristic" that distinguishes a flat drill's performance limitations.

Based on these technical aspects, the most defining characteristic of a flat drill is that it is cheap to make, but it fails significantly in the area of chip evacuation.

**Hence, the correct characteristic is that its production is inexpensive, but its chip removal capability is poor.**</p
